hints: Look closely at what is formed and what you start from, elements in their normal states or one mole of fuel burning?
Notice the equation makes exactly 1 mole of $\text{Na}_2\text{O(s)}$ from $\text{Na(s)}$ and $\text{O}_2\text{(g)}$, both elements in their standard states.
Remember that giving out heat means exothermic with negative $\Delta H$, and check whether the mole ratio fits formation (1 mole product) or combustion (1 mole reactant burned).
walkthrough:
**Use the heat clue**

Sodium burns giving out heat energy. That is the language of an exothermic reaction.

For exothermic, heat is lost to surroundings, so:
$$\Delta H^\circ < 0$$

**Recall standard enthalpy of formation**

Standard enthalpy of formation, $\Delta H_f^\circ$, is the enthalpy change when 1 mole of a compound is formed from its elements in their standard states.

Check our equation:
$$2\text{Na(s)} + \tfrac{1}{2}\text{O}_2\text{(g)} \rightarrow \text{Na}_2\text{O(s)}$$

**Match the definition perfectly**

We make exactly 1 mole of $\text{Na}_2\text{O(s)}$. The reactants are $\text{Na(s)}$ and $\text{O}_2\text{(g)}$, which are the elements Na and O in their standard states at 298 K and 1 atm.

So this is exactly the formation equation for sodium oxide.

**See why combustion is different**

Standard enthalpy of combustion, $\Delta H_c^\circ$, is the enthalpy change when 1 mole of a substance burns completely in oxygen.

Here we burn 2 moles of Na, not 1 mole. For 1 mole of Na the equation would need halving, so this given equation cannot be the combustion equation for sodium.

options.A: Not correct. $\text{Na}_2\text{O}$ is an ionic lattice, not discrete covalent $\text{Na-O}$ molecules. Its $\Delta H^\circ$ involves atomisation of Na, bond dissociation of $\text{O}_2$, ionisation energies, electron affinities and lattice energy, not just forming two covalent bonds. The sign would also be wrong as bond making is exothermic.
options.B: Not correct. The question states heat energy is given out, so the reaction is exothermic. Exothermic reactions have negative $\Delta H^\circ$, not positive.
options.C: Not correct. Combustion must be for 1 mole of the fuel burned. Here 2 moles of $\text{Na(s)}$ are burned. The combustion of sodium would be $\text{Na(s)} + \tfrac{1}{4}\text{O}_2\text{(g)} \rightarrow \tfrac{1}{2}\text{Na}_2\text{O(s)}$. This is a common trap confusing formation with combustion.
options.D: Correct. The equation shows 1 mole of $\text{Na}_2\text{O(s)}$ formed from its elements, $\text{Na(s)}$ and $\text{O}_2\text{(g)}$, in their standard states under standard conditions. That is exactly the definition of standard enthalpy change of formation.
